Connectome-constrained networks predict neural activity across the fly visual system. Nature 634(8036):1132-1140 (2024). doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07939-3. PMCID PMC11525180, PMID 39261740. Received 16 Mar 2023, accepted 9 Aug 2024, published 11 Sep 2024. CC BY 4.0 (verified via Crossref licence field and the JATS licence element).

sources.what_was_read: Read the whole main text: abstract, all Results sections and the Discussion. Read the whole Methods: connectome construction, neuronal dynamics, parameter counting, scatter/gather implementation, optic-flow task, Sintel dataset, fly-eye rendering, augmentation, decoder, EPE, ablation definitions, unconstrained-CNN baseline, flash and moving-edge stimuli, FRI and DSI definitions, the DS threshold, UMAP clustering, receptive fields, maximally excitatory stimuli, model selection and the synthetic MNIST experiments. Also read every figure and Extended Data figure caption, the data and code availability statements and the reference list. I could not see the figure images themselves, so numbers that appear only in plots (for example the median correlations in Fig. 2d) are not available to me. The SI PDF (Supplementary Notes 1-5), the Supplementary Data zip and the Peer Review File were NOT read because each is larger than 5 MB (see the separate source entry).

key_findings.finding: Model scale. The network has 64 identified cell types (65 node types, because the CT1 compartments in medulla and lobula are counted separately), 45,669 neurons and 1,513,231 connections, on a hexagonal lattice of 721 columns (31 columns across) covering the central visual field of the right eye. Each model neuron corresponds to a real cell type and column.
key_findings.numbers: 64 (65) types; 45,669 neurons; 1,513,231 connections; 721 columns

key_findings.finding: Connectome source. Two FlyEM FIB-SEM datasets were merged: FIB-25 (7 medulla columns, 702 neurons) and FIB-19 (whole optic lobe, 1,099 neurons), giving 1,801 neurons. About 830 neurons had hand-annotated column positions, 722 of them in simulated types. No T5 cell was annotated, so columns were assigned by a probabilistic EM algorithm. The local reconstructions were then tiled with perfect periodicity (translation invariance), so every pair of neurons with the same pre/post type and the same relative offset gets the same synapse count. Cited sources: Takemura 2015 PNAS, Takemura 2017 eLife, Shinomiya 2019 eLife, Shinomiya 2022 Curr Biol, Rivera-Alba 2011. This is a single consensus connectome, not a set of connectomes from multiple individuals.
key_findings.numbers: 1,801 neurons (702 + 1,099); ~830 reference positions; 722 in simulated types

key_findings.finding: What is trained. Only 734 parameters are free: 65 membrane time constants and 65 resting potentials (one of each per cell type), plus 604 non-negative unitary-synapse scale factors alpha (one per type-to-type connection). What is fixed from the connectome: 604 signs and 2,355 synapse-count filter entries (the average synapse count per type pair and hexagonal offset). Weights are w_ij = alpha * sigma * N(t_i, t_j, du, dv). Signs come from transmitter/receptor profiling (mainly Davis et al. 2020 transcriptomics). Histaminergic, GABAergic and glutamatergic outputs are hyperpolarizing and cholinergic outputs depolarizing. R8 is assigned per target according to ort expression. For a minority of cell types the authors used 'guesses of plausible transmitter phenotypes'. All 50 models start from the same initial values: alpha = 0.01/<N>, tau = 50 ms, V_rest ~ N(0.5, 0.05) a.u. During Euler integration tau is clamped to at least dt.
key_findings.numbers: 734 = 65 + 65 + 604; 604 signs and 2,355 counts fixed

key_findings.finding: Dynamics. Neurons are passive leaky linear, non-spiking, single-compartment point neurons, except CT1, which has one compartment per column. The equation is tau * dV/dt = -V + sum_j s_ij + V_rest + e_i. Synapses release instantaneously and graded through a threshold-linear (ReLU) function. External input e_i goes only to R1-R8. The model has no electrical synapses, no synaptic dynamics or depression, and no neuromodulation.

Training task. The task is optic-flow regression on MPI Sintel: 23 sequences of 20-50 frames at 24 fps and 1,024x436 px. Frames are converted to greyscale, and each of the 721 hex columns averages a 13x13-pixel patch, with columns 13 px apart. Training uses 19-frame chunks (792 ms) resampled to 50 Hz (dt = 20 ms). Augmentations: hexagonal flips and rotations, Gaussian noise with sigma_n = 0.08, log-contrast variance 0.04 and brightness variance 0.01. The decoder is feedforward and convolutional: 5x5 kernels mapping the rectified instantaneous voltages of D = 34 output cell types to 8 channels and then 3 channels (two flow components plus a shared normalization). The loss is the L2 norm. Optimizer: Adam (beta1 0.9, beta2 0.999) with learning rate stepped from 5e-5 to 5e-6 in 10 steps, batch size 4, and about 250,000 iterations before the models generalized. An activity regularizer on the resting potentials (lambda_V = 0.1, a = 5, gamma = 1, delta = 0.01) ran for 150,000 iterations. Models were checkpointed on held-out Sintel clips by EPE. The task-error lower bound came from an unconstrained CNN baseline: 5 CNNs with 414,666 parameters each.
key_findings.numbers: 23 sequences; dt 20 ms; batch 4; ~250k iterations; decoder 34->8->3 channels; CNN 414,666 params x 5

key_findings.finding: Ensemble. 50 models were trained under the same constraints and the analysis focuses on the 10 with the best task performance. On task error, the ensemble beats both the decoder alone and models with random parameters (Extended Data Fig. 2a).
key_findings.numbers: 50 models; top 10 analysed

key_findings.finding: ON/OFF contrast preference. The ensemble-median FRI gives the correct preference for all 32 cell types whose contrast preference is experimentally established. The task-optimal model gets 30 of 32. Across all 50 models, the predictions for 29 of 31 cell types are individually significant (binomial test, P < 0.05; the paper writes 31 here and 32 elsewhere). The model also predicts contrast preference for the remaining 33 types, and those predictions are not yet tested.
key_findings.numbers: 32/32 (ensemble median); 30/32 (task-optimal model); 29/31 significant

key_findings.finding: Direction selectivity. In response to ON/OFF edges in 12 directions at 6 speeds (13.92-145 deg/s), T4 comes out ON-direction-selective and T5 OFF-direction-selective. The T4/T5 inputs Mi1, Tm3, Mi4, Mi9, Tm1, Tm2, Tm4, Tm9 and CT1 come out correctly non-selective. 19 cell types receive asymmetric multicolumnar input, but only 12 are predicted to be DS: T4a-d, T5a-d, TmY3, TmY4, TmY5a and TmY18. The DS threshold d_thresh = 0.357 is the 99% quantile of permutation DSIs from symmetric-input types, followed by a binomial test against p = 0.1. TmY3 is proposed as a parallel motion pathway, but this has not been tested experimentally. The spatial offset of inputs does not correlate strongly with DSI.
key_findings.numbers: 12 of 19 asymmetric types predicted DS; d_thresh = 0.357

key_findings.finding: Ablations of the constraints (Fig. 2d, Extended Data Fig. 2; 50 models per variant, top 10 compared). (a) Random DMN (full connectome, random Gaussian cell and synapse parameters, only the decoder trained): contrast preference is accurate, but DS and preferred direction (PD) are poor. (b) Cell-type connectivity only: poor predictions. (c)-(f) Optimizing synapse counts, or single-cell connectivity within a 3-column radius, or signs, or counts plus signs: FRI is accurate whenever signs are given; DSI (but not PD) is accurate with known single-cell connectivity even without synapse counts. (g) Merging the T4 and T5 subtypes (58 types) costs nothing. (h) Merging into E (37 types), I (22) and mixed (4) types performs as badly as the random DMN. There is NO ablation with a shuffled or random connectome (degree- or count-preserving) plus task training, and NO ablation with an alternative training task.

Task error and tuning realism are linked. Models with lower task error predict the DSI of T4/T5 and their inputs better: r = 0.60, P = 2.6e-6 in the main text. Extended Data Fig. 2e gives r = -0.60 (task error vs correlation), 95% CI [-1, -0.42], df = 48. The FRI correlation with known polarity did NOT increase significantly with task performance.

Degeneracy and clustering. UMAP plus a Gaussian mixture (2-5 components, chosen by BIC) applied to responses to naturalistic scenes finds clusters for many cell types. For T4c there are 3 clusters: up-tuned (correct, mean task error 5.297), down-tuned (5.316) and untuned (5.357). Preferred direction is tied to the polarity of Mi4 and Mi9, so connectome plus task does not uniquely fix PD. Keeping only models consistent with the measured T4c tuning is enough to fix Mi4 and Mi9 polarity. TmY3 shows 4 clusters (5.298, 5.317, 5.328, 5.331).
key_findings.numbers: T4c cluster errors 5.297 / 5.316 / 5.357

key_findings.finding: Predicted mechanisms in the task-optimal cluster. T4 combines fast excitation (Mi1, Tm3) with offset, delayed inhibition (Mi4, plus CT1). T5 relies on delayed CT1(Lo1) inhibition plus Tm9/Tm1 excitation. The model predicts lateral T4-T4 and T5-T5 excitation between cells with the same preferred direction; this is new and untested. It shows null-direction suppression without preferred-direction enhancement, consistent with voltage data (Gruntman 2018/2019). Spatial receptive fields: Tm3 and Tm4 broad (2-column radius, 11.6 deg), others narrow (5.8 deg). Temporal flash responses are correct except for Tm4, which is wrongly predicted to depolarize.
key_findings.numbers: 11.6 deg vs 5.8 deg RF radius

key_findings.finding: Synthetic sparsity experiment. Ground-truth networks were feedforward MNIST classifiers with 6 hidden layers of 128 units, Dale's law, and lottery-ticket pruning, with 25 ground-truth networks per sparsity level. Re-fitting with known binary connectivity reached a median Pearson r of 0.85 at 10% connectivity but only 0.38 at 80%. With known connectivity plus noisy strengths (uniform multiplicative noise, sigma = 0.5, used as an L2 prior), r was > 0.9 at all densities.
key_findings.numbers: r 0.85 (10%) vs 0.38 (80%); > 0.9 with strengths

key_findings.finding: Authors' claim not directly tested: they say the fly model lies 'between the two curves' of the synthetic experiment, and they attribute its success to sparsity plus synapse-count-derived strengths. The fly circuit itself was not tested at different sparsity levels.

The ON/OFF (FRI) result is largely fixed by the sign constraints and the input injection, not by the task. Three points support this: the authors' own random-parameter DMN already predicts contrast preference accurately; 8 of the 32 'known' types are photoreceptors (R1-R8), which receive the luminance input directly; and the polarity of lamina cells follows from the histaminergic sign. So the evidence that depends on the task is essentially the T4/T5 DS and PD results (8 types), the non-DS of about 10 input types, and 8 tuning curves.

The validation targets are literature-derived summary labels, not raw recordings. They are hard-coded in flyvis/utils/groundtruth_utils.py: ternary polarity (32 non-zero types), binary on/off DS and non-DS lists, cardinal preferred directions for T4a-d and T5a-d (180, 0, 90, 270 deg), and 8 tuning curves of 12 directions each, digitized from Maisak et al. 2013 Fig. 3g,h (calcium imaging). There is no held-out individual, developmental stage or perturbation/intervention dataset.

About 9% of the fixed 'synapse counts' appear to be imputed rather than measured. The default connectome config sets n_syn_fill = 1, which fills unknown offsets inside the convex hull of each filter with 1 synapse. The shipped JSON has 605 type pairs (the paper says 604) and 2,140 raw offset entries. My pure-Python recomputation of the hull fill gives 2,287 (interior only) to 2,385 (interior plus boundary) entries, which brackets the paper's 2,355.
key_findings.numbers: 2,140 raw entries; 2,287-2,385 after fill vs 2,355 reported

sources.model_or_method_spec: Inputs: greyscale Sintel video rendered onto 721 hex columns and added to R1-R8. Fixed: cell-type identities (65 node types), hexagonal tiling and translation invariance, filter synapse counts N(t_i, t_j, du, dv) (2,355 entries, about 9% apparently hull-filled with 1), 604 signs from transmitter/receptor profiling plus guesses, ReLU graded release, Euler dt = 20 ms (training) or 5-10 ms (analysis), and the decoder architecture. Fitted: 65 tau, 65 V_rest and 604 alpha >= 0, plus the decoder weights, trained end-to-end by BPTT on the optic-flow L2 loss, with an activity regularizer on V_rest. No neural-activity data enter training. Biology enters as priors through the connectome counts and the signs. The paper does not use the term 'priors supplied by authors', but expert choices include the 64 types, which 34 output types feed the decoder, sign guesses for some types, the periodicity assumption, and the decision to read out only from medulla and downstream types.
sources.validation_design: Nothing biological was held out in the sense of individuals, stages or edges. Validation compares simulated responses to standard probes (circular flashes of radius 6 columns, moving edges in 12 directions x 6 speeds x ON/OFF, single-ommatidium flashes of 5-300 ms, moving and static bars, maximally excitatory stimuli) with results from 26 previously published studies (Supplementary Data 5 and 6, not read). Metrics: FRI sign agreement plus a binomial test; Pearson correlation of predicted T4/T5 tuning curves with one measured curve per subtype, taking the maximum over 6 speeds; correlation of DSI with binary DS labels; angular distance of the PD; qualitative RF width and temporal-kernel comparisons. The model is never fit to neural data, which gives it some independence from the targets. But it is not blind: the targets were well-known literature results available to the authors when they designed the model. Model ranking used task error, which is non-biological. However, Extended Data Figs. 4, 7 and 8 explicitly select models using empirical tuning data, and Fig. 3 shows filtering by measured T4c tuning. Baselines: random-parameter DMN, 5 DMNs with reduced connectome constraints, 2 cell-type merges, and an unconstrained CNN (task error only). Missing: shuffled or randomized connectome with task training, a different task, a non-connectome network of matched size, and earlier models such as Mano et al. 2021, which is cited as related work but not compared.
stated_limitations: The models of neurons and synapses are reductionist. They cannot account for electrical synapses, nonlinear chemical synapses or neuromodulation.
Only motion computation is used as the task, and it is 'but one of many computations' of the visual system.
The connectome is a consensus built by assuming perfect periodicity. Neuronal superposition is ignored in the hexagonal CNN.
No transmitter data were available for a minority of cell types, so their signs are guesses.
Connectome and task may not uniquely constrain the parameters, which is why an ensemble is used. Preferred direction can come out opposite in some local optima (the T4c clusters).
FRI only says whether a cell depolarizes to ON or OFF. It misses unrectified cells (R1-R8, L1, L2).
Estimates of spatial asymmetry from existing reconstructions can be noisy.
How well connection strength can be inferred from noisy synapse counts is still unknown.
The temporal flash response of Tm4 is mispredicted (depolarization predicted).
Voltages and currents are in arbitrary units, so responses must be normalized before averaging across models.
sources.code: https://github.com/TuragaLab/flyvis, MIT licence (verified via GitHub API /license). See the flyvis code-repository entry for install requirements and CPU feasibility.
sources.data: The paper's data availability statement points to the GitHub repo for 'data, trained models and interactive notebooks'. Supplementary Data are on Nature as a zip of 26,522,689 bytes (HEAD-verified; not downloaded because it exceeds 5 MB). It contains: type-to-type filters (average synapse counts), connectome source references, the type connection matrix, a single-neuron connectome for 91 columns, the 26 activity-study references with BibTeX, and the prediction catalogue for 64 types. The connectome JSON (618,148 bytes) also ships in the flyvis package. The licence of the underlying FlyEM FIB-25 and FIB-19 data is unverified.
sources.novelty_threat_for_m08: High for any M08 G-FUNCTION claim in the fly motion pathway. It already shows that a connectome-constrained, task-optimized network with about 734 cell-type-level parameters predicts ON/OFF polarity, T4/T5 direction selectivity and preferred directions, and input-cell kinetics without fitting neural data. It also already covers: the connectome-driven parameter reduction (2.2e9 to 734); ensembles plus clustering as a way to express degeneracy and generate hypotheses; the 'sparsity makes connectome constraints identifiable' argument (synthetic MNIST); and ablations of which connectome measurements (signs, counts, single-cell connectivity) matter. Any M08 result of the form 'connectome plus task optimization predicts T4/T5 tuning' would be a replication. It does NOT pre-empt: a discovered generative rule for structure (the periodic tiling and averaged filters are hand-imposed or measured, not learned); transfer across individuals or connectomes; development or stages; validated perturbation or intervention predictions; or G-CONSTRUCT, generating new circuits from capability constraints (topology is fixed and only scalars are trained).
sources.gaps_m08_could_test: (1) Null connectomes with task training. Shuffle filter offsets within type pairs; swap type labels; use a degree- or count-preserving random wiring; or mirror the spatial offsets of the T4/T5 inputs, which should flip PD if the structure is causal. The paper has none of these. (2) A zero-parameter sign-parity baseline for ON/OFF: propagate signs along paths from R1-R8 and count how many of the 32 polarities it predicts with no training. This tests H0-PRIOR. (3) A task-swap control: same connectome trained on luminance reconstruction, next-frame prediction or a non-motion task, to test whether DS needs the motion task or only temporal integration. (4) Cross-connectome transfer: rebuild the filters from FlyWire right optic lobe (Matsliah et al. 2024) or the Nern et al. 2025 optic-lobe connectome (different individuals) and check whether the same 734-parameter recipe reproduces the predictions. (5) Compress the 2,355-entry filter table into a parametric generative rule (for example a per-type-pair offset distribution) and measure how much functional prediction survives. This links G-STRUCT to G-FUNCTION. (6) Zero-shot perturbation predictions from the frozen released ensemble (silencing of Mi1, Tm3, Mi4 or Mi9, CT1, Tm9), checked against published intervention studies that were not used in their validation. CPU evaluation of the released ensemble should be enough for this. (7) Quantitative rather than binary comparison (DSI magnitudes, temporal kernels) with ensemble-level uncertainty, where raw data exist.

sources.citation: TuragaLab/flyvis: official implementation of Lappalainen et al. 2024 (GitHub repository, PyPI package 'flyvis' v1.2.0, documentation at turagalab.github.io/flyvis). Repository copyright line: Lappalainen, Tschopp, McGill, Macke, Turaga (2023).
sources.what_was_read: Read in full: GitHub API repo metadata and licence endpoint; the full recursive file tree with sizes; readme.md; pyproject.toml; CHANGELOG.md; .env.example; docs/docs/install.md, index.md and faq.md (repo source of the docs site); .github/workflows/auto_test.yml; flyvis/__init__.py; flyvis_cli/download_pretrained_models.py and flyvis_cli.py (first 120 lines); all default Hydra configs (network, connectome, dynamics, edge sign/count/strength, node bias/time constant, task, optim, penalizer, scheduler, solver); flyvis/network/dynamics.py; flyvis/analysis/validation.py; flyvis/utils/groundtruth_utils.py; the fill_hull and add_edges functions in connectome.py; the structure of connectome/fib25-fib19_v2.2.json, analysed locally; and the code cells of the Fig. 2 notebook. Partly read: initialization.py and sintel_utils.py, by grep. Rendered docs pages read with WebFetch: the CLI reference and the Fig. 2 example. Release and PyPI metadata were read. I installed nothing, ran nothing and downloaded no pretrained data.

key_findings.finding: Licence: MIT. The GitHub API reports spdx_id MIT, and the licence text names Lappalainen, Tschopp, McGill, Macke and Turaga (2023). PyPI classifiers also say MIT, although the PyPI 'license' field is empty. Repo snapshot on 2026-10-25: 207 stars, 40 forks, 2 open issues/PRs, last push 2026-10-14, latest release v1.2.0 (2026-08-06), not archived.

Install requirements. requires-python is >=3.9,<3.13, and CI tests Python 3.9, 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12 on ubuntu-latest. torch and torchvision are listed unpinned. Other dependencies: numba, datamate, scipy, matplotlib, networkx, scikit-learn, umap-learn, ffmpeg-python, hydra-core, xarray, pandas, google-api-python-client, among others. An optional 'pretrained' extra pins numba==0.55.2, matplotlib==3.7.1, scikit-learn==1.1.1, umap-learn==0.5.3, xarray==2023.7.0, pandas==2.2.2 and joblib==1.3.2. PyPI files: wheel of 385,602 bytes and sdist of 30,073,117 bytes. The GitHub API size field is 192,865 (KB under GitHub's convention; the unit is from my general knowledge).
Possible version conflict: the numba==0.55.2 pin in the 'pretrained' extra probably restricts that extra to Python versions of 3.10 or older. Unverified.

CPU inference. flyvis/__init__.py picks CUDA if it is available and otherwise CPU, and sets that as the default torch device. The CI workflow runs on GitHub's standard ubuntu-latest runners (no GPU): it downloads the pretrained models and runs the test suite with -m 'not require_large_download and not gpu'. A 2026 third-party PR (#28) reports 21 require_download tests passing against the pretrained models. The Colab notebooks say you can 'proceed on CPU (slow)'. The v1.2.0 changelog says that shipping the response-normalization constants (responses_norm.h5, 57,480 bytes) 'makes the paper figures reproducible on a laptop'. Issue/PR #24 says computing those constants needs about 30 minutes of simulated naturalistic stimuli per model, which is 'infeasible on a laptop' for the whole ensemble.

My CPU feasibility assessment. Evaluating the released 50-model ensemble on flashes, moving edges and custom stimuli should be feasible on a laptop CPU (minutes to about an hour), because one forward step is about 1.5M edge multiply-adds per sample. Simulating long naturalistic stimuli for all 50 models is slow but possible. Retraining is GPU territory. A rough estimate from the third-party PR #27 benchmark (RTX 5090: batch 16, 32 steps, 48 ms forward/backward, 3.641 GiB peak) and 250k iterations at batch 4 is on the order of a few GPU-hours per model, so roughly 100-300 GPU-hours for a 50-model ensemble. On CPU, one model would probably take days. These are estimates, not measurements.

Training memory. A maintainer (lappalainenj, in issue #13) says one training job uses 'no more than 1GB of CPU RAM and 3GB of video RAM in our environment'. Neither the paper's main text nor its Methods states GPU-hours.

Pretrained data. 'flyvis download-pretrained' fetches two zips from a Google Drive folder through the Google Drive API: results_pretrained_models.zip (SHA256 71c78d40...81db1) and results_umap_and_clustering.zip. The downloader authenticates with an API key hard-coded in flyvis_cli/download_pretrained_models.py. I did not run it, because of the no-credential rule and the unknown file sizes. The archive sizes are not documented anywhere I looked (README, docs, code, releases, PyPI) and remain unverified. The tests and docs only reference the ensemble 'flow/0000', with 50 models named flow/0000/000-049. The docs Fig. 2 page loads 50 networks and selects the top 10: 000, 001, 002, 003, 004, 005, 007, 009, 006, 013.

Ablation ensembles probably are not released. The random-parameter DMN and the reduced-constraint DMNs of Fig. 2d do not appear in the docs or tests. Only flow/0000 is referenced. Unverified, because I could not inspect the archive.

Sintel is needed for training and for naturalistic stimuli only. The code downloads MPI-Sintel-complete.zip from files.is.tue.mpg.de over plain HTTP, without login. A HEAD request gave Content-Length 5,627,783,629 bytes (about 5.6 GB). If a depth task is requested, MPI-Sintel-depth-training-20150305.zip (1,601,251,750 bytes) is also fetched. Flash, moving-edge and custom-stimulus analyses with pretrained models do not need Sintel.

Default config matches the paper. Signs: requires_grad false, grouped by type pair. Synapse counts: requires_grad false, grouped by type pair and offset. Synapse strength: requires_grad true, scale 0.01, clamped non-negative. Resting potential: Normal with mean 0.5 and std 0.05 (the paper writes 'variance 0.05'), trainable, with an activity penalty. Time constant: 0.05 s, trainable. Other settings: dt 0.02, batch 4, n_iters 250,000, learning rate 5e-5 to 5e-6 in 10 steps, activity penalty with baseline 5.0, weight 0.1, stopping at 150,000 iterations, below/above weights 1.0/0.1. Decoder: DecoderGAVP with shape [8, 2], kernel 5, dropout 0.5. Sintel split: 4 folds, fold 1, original_split true.

Connectome JSON (fib25-fib19_v2.2.json, 618,148 bytes) contents: 65 nodes; 605 chemical edges (type pairs); 2,140 offset entries with fractional mean synapse counts; 377 positive and 228 negative signs. Sign provenance, from the 'alpha_references' field: NernPC2018 on 286 edges and ReiserPC2017 on 82 edges (these labels look like personal communications), Hardie1989 on 40, Karuppudurai2014 on 12, Lin2016 on 12, and no reference on 267 edges. 8 input units (R1-R8) and 34 decoder output units (T1-T5d, Tm and TmY types).

How the counts above should be read. The sign labels in the shipped JSON partly rest on personal communications, while the paper says it relied 'primarily' on Davis et al. 2020. How the two map onto each other is unverified. My pure-Python recomputation of the hull fill (n_syn_fill = 1) gives 2,287-2,385 filter entries, consistent with the 2,355 reported.

The official Fig. 2 notebook has the comment '# TODO: fix this, does not come out as expected' above the DSI-correlation computation (dsi_correlation_to_known). Third-party PR #28 (merged 2026-10-14) fixed tuning-curve and PD matching, which matched by position rather than by cell type. With the default neuron order the results were bit-identical. The PR author reports a correlation of 0.95 between the T4a ON-edge tuning of pretrained model flow/0000/000 and the known curve.
key_findings.numbers: T4a correlation 0.95 (third party)

sources.model_or_method_spec: PPNeuronIGRSynapses dynamics: tau * dV/dt = -V + bias + sum(sign * syn_count * syn_strength * ReLU(V_src)) + x_t, with tau clamped to at least dt. Graph built by ConnectomeFromAvgFilters with extent 15 and n_syn_fill 1. The Hydra configs expose every parameter group's requires_grad, so the code can directly express the ablations (train signs or counts, alter groupby). Training, validation, recording and analysis are available through the 'flyvis' CLI, with slurm/LSF/virtual-cluster support.
sources.validation_design: Software tests only: pytest with markers slow, gpu, require_download and require_large_download. The released biological 'ground truth' is the label set in groundtruth_utils.py (polarity, DS lists, preferred directions, Maisak 2013 tuning curves), and the analysis functions fri_correlation_to_known, dsi_correlation_to_known, correlation_to_known_tuning_curves and angular_distance_to_known score models against it.
stated_limitations: The docs FAQ is empty ('We have not created a formal FAQ yet').
Package status is 'Development Status :: 3 - Alpha'.

Before v1.2.0, the response normalization had to be recomputed for every model (about 30 minutes of naturalistic simulation each), which made the paper figures 'effectively unreproducible outside a cluster' (issue #24).
Training OOM on slurm was reported in issue #13 and not root-caused. The maintainer attributes it to the user's environment.
Python 3.13 is not supported (PR #15 still open).
sources.code: MIT (GitHub API). Python >=3.9,<3.13. PyTorch with an unpinned version. Installs from PyPI as 'pip install flyvis'. CPU fallback is automatic, and inference on pretrained models is feasible on CPU (author CI evidence plus my assessment). Training realistically needs a GPU: a few GPU-hours per model by my estimate, which is unverified.
sources.data: Bundled with the package: the connectome JSON (618,148 B) and responses_norm.h5 (57,480 B). The pretrained ensemble flow/0000 (50 models) and the UMAP/clustering results come from Google Drive through an API-key downloader; sizes unverified. Their licence is MIT according to a maintainer reply in issue #26 (2026-09-29), which says MIT covers the archive, derived arrays and generated videos/traces, with attribution to the Nature paper. There is no licence file inside the archive (per the issue author). Sintel (5.6 GB) is downloaded automatically, without login, only for training or naturalistic stimuli.
sources.novelty_threat_for_m08: It provides a ready-made, MIT-licensed, CPU-runnable connectome-constrained functional model of the fly motion pathway. Using it as M08's 'functional evidence line' counts as reproduction or reuse, not discovery. Any M08 functional claim that does not beat or extend this released ensemble against the same groundtruth_utils labels cannot be called novel.
sources.gaps_m08_could_test: With the pretrained ensemble on CPU, M08 could run three tests with no training: (a) a sign-parity-only baseline against the 32 polarity labels; (b) frozen-model perturbation predictions (zeroing a cell type's output) compared with published silencing results not used in their validation; (c) sensitivity of the predictions to imputed (hull-filled) filter entries, by setting n_syn_fill = 0, which is a config change but requires retraining to be fair. Experiments that need GPU retraining (a §10A request): shuffled or mirrored connectomes, task swaps, FlyWire-derived filters, and compressed generative filter rules.

read:lappalainen.summary_for_m08:
Lappalainen et al. (Nature 2024; full main text and Methods read via PMC/Europe PMC; SI, Supplementary Data and Peer Review File not read because each exceeds 5 MB) is the canonical connectome-constrained functional model of the fly motion pathway.

Model. Structure is fixed:
- 64 cell types (65 node types with the two CT1 compartments), 45,669 neurons, 1,513,231 connections and 721 hex columns.
- The connectome is a single consensus built from FlyEM FIB-25 (7 medulla columns) and FIB-19 (whole optic lobe), 1,801 reconstructed neurons in all, tiled with perfect periodicity.
- 2,355 average synapse-count filter entries are fixed. From the code, about 9% of them appear to be hull-filled imputations of 1 synapse (my inference).
- 604 type-pair signs are fixed. They come from transmitter/receptor profiling, guesses for some types, and in the shipped JSON partly from personal communications.

Only 734 scalars are trained: 65 time constants, 65 resting potentials and 604 non-negative unitary-synapse scales. A 2-layer convolutional decoder reads the 34 output types. Training is end-to-end BPTT on Sintel optic flow (23 sequences, dt 20 ms, batch 4, about 250k iterations, 50 models from identical initial values). No neural data enter training.

Biological validation compares the models with literature results from 26 studies, encoded in flyvis as summary labels: ternary ON/OFF polarity for 32 types, binary DS lists, cardinal PDs, and 8 T4/T5 tuning curves digitized from Maisak 2013. Results:
- The ensemble-median FRI gets 32/32 polarities right (task-optimal model 30/32).
- T4 comes out ON-DS and T5 OFF-DS, and the T4/T5 inputs come out non-DS.
- 12 of 19 types with asymmetric input are predicted DS, including untested predictions for TmY3, TmY4, TmY5a and TmY18.
- Lower task error goes with more realistic DSI (r = 0.60, P = 2.6e-6). FRI realism does not improve with task error.
- Tm4 kinetics are mispredicted.

Their ablations:
- Random parameters on the full connectome still predict polarity, but not DS or PD.
- Cell-type connectivity alone is poor.
- Signs are needed for polarity. Single-cell connectivity without synapse counts gives DS but not PD.
- Merging into E/I types fails. Merging T4/T5 subtypes is harmless.
- T4c clustering shows that connectome plus task leaves PD ambiguous: up and down solutions differ only slightly in task error (5.297 vs 5.316). Measured Mi4/Mi9 polarity resolves it.
- A synthetic MNIST study shows that sparsity improves identifiability (median r 0.85 at 10% connectivity vs 0.38 at 80%).

What is missing for M08's purposes:
- No shuffled, randomized or mirrored connectome trained on the task.
- No alternative task.
- No size-matched non-connectome network compared on tuning.
- No cross-individual connectome, no developmental data, no perturbation or intervention data.
- No blind or held-out biological targets.

My reading: the polarity result is largely implied by the sign constraints and the input injection (their own random-parameter baseline already gets it, and 8 of the 32 targets are photoreceptors). The evidence that genuinely depends on the task therefore rests on about 8 T4/T5 types plus about 10 non-DS input types.

flyvis software:
- MIT licence (GitHub API). The maintainer says in issue #26 that MIT also covers the pretrained weights.
- Python >=3.9,<3.13. torch and torchvision unpinned. pip install flyvis (v1.2.0, 2026-08-06).
- Automatic CPU fallback. CI runs the pretrained-model tests on GPU-less runners. Laptop reproduction of the figures has been possible since v1.2.0.
- The pretrained ensemble flow/0000 (50 models) comes from Google Drive via a downloader with a hard-coded API key. Archive size is unverified and I did not run it.
- Training needs Sintel (5,627,783,629 bytes, HEAD-verified), downloaded automatically.
- Training is GPU-scale: the maintainer gives at most 3 GB VRAM per job. My estimate is a few GPU-hours per model, which is unverified. A 96 GB GPU is not justified by flyvis.

Novelty threat for M08: high. Any G-FUNCTION claim that 'connectome plus task predicts T4/T5 tuning' is a replication of this work. The paper also already covers the ensemble/degeneracy analysis and the sparsity-identifiability argument. It does not touch discovered generative structural rules, cross-individual or stage transfer, validated perturbation predictions, or G-CONSTRUCT.

An independent re-test of 'connectivity + task predicts tuning' would need the following:
1. Pre-registered biological targets the authors did not use. Candidates are new cell types or studies outside their 26, perturbation or silencing data, or quantitative kinetics, all frozen before evaluation, with ensemble-level uncertainty and matched metrics (not binary labels alone).
2. A zero-training sign-parity baseline for polarity, to measure how much the task adds (H0-PRIOR).
3. Null connectomes trained identically: offset-shuffled filters, type-label-shuffled filters, count-preserving random wiring, and mirrored T4/T5 input offsets (which predict a PD flip if the structure is causal).
4. Task-swap controls (non-motion objective) and stimulus-set swaps.
5. A size-matched non-connectome recurrent network and the prior model of Mano et al. 2021 as baselines.
6. Rebuilding the filters from an independent connectome (FlyWire right optic lobe, Matsliah et al. 2024, or the Nern et al. 2025 optic lobe) to test transfer across individuals.
7. For a generative-law angle: replacing the 2,355-entry filter table with a compact parametric rule and measuring how much functional prediction survives.

Items 2 and the frozen-model perturbation tests run on CPU with the released ensemble. Items 3-7 need retraining on the order of tens to hundreds of GPU-hours (my estimate), which would have to go through the §10A process, plus user approval for the downloads above 5 MB: Sintel at about 5.6 GB, and the pretrained archive, whose size is unverified.

sources.citation: Shiu PK, Sterne GR, Spiller N, Franconville R, ... Seeds AM, Scott K. A Drosophila computational brain model reveals sensorimotor processing. Nature 634(8032):210-219 (2024). doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07763-9. PMCID PMC11446845, PMID 39358519. Received 26 Jul 2023, accepted 27 Jun 2024, published 2 Oct 2024. Preprint: bioRxiv 10.1101/2023.05.02.539144 (2 May 2023). Licence CC BY 4.0, read from the PMC XML licence statement.
sources.url: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07763-9 (the page redirected to an idp.nature.com cookie flow, so the full text was read from https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC11446845/fullTextXML instead)
sources.what_was_read: Complete article text from the Europe PMC full-text XML: abstract, main results, discussion, all Methods (computational model, neurotransmitter assignment, robustness, modelling limitations, GRN classification, split-GAL4 identification, grooming modelling, optogenetics, silencing, calcium imaging, statistics), data and code availability, competing interests, and the captions of all 4 Extended Data figures (images not viewed). I also opened the Supplementary Tables xlsx (2,539,037 bytes, under the 5 MB limit) with a stdlib parser and read ST1D (shuffled connectivity), ST3 (106-cell-type screen), ST9A/9B (raw behavioural counts), ST10 (overall prediction tally) and the ST11A-F robustness totals. Not read: Reporting Summary PDF (3.1 MB) and the peer-review file (not checked).

key_findings.finding: Model: leaky integrate-and-fire with an exponentially decaying conductance-like variable g (dv/dt=(g-(v-Vrest))/Tm; dg/dt=-g/tau; g += w_ji on each presynaptic spike), simulated in Brian2. It includes all proofread neurons of FlyWire materialization v630. Every neuron is identical and baseline firing is 0 Hz.
key_findings.numbers: 127,400 neurons; Vrest=-52 mV, Vreset=-52 mV, Vth=-45 mV, Rm=10 kOhm cm2, Cm=2 uF cm-2 (Tm=20 ms), tau_syn=5 ms, refractory 2.2 ms, delay 1.8 ms, Wsyn=0.275 mV

key_findings.finding: What is fixed from the connectome: w_ji = (FlyWire synapse count j->i) x (+1 or -1) x Wsyn. The sign is a per-neuron rule applied to Eckstein et al. 2024 synapse-level transmitter predictions: cleft score cutoff 50, the top prediction at each presynaptic site, and the neuron is inhibitory if more than half its presynaptic sites are GABA or Glu. DA, OA and 5-HT neurons count as excitatory. Excitatory and inhibitory synapses have equal magnitude.
key_findings.numbers: Whole volume: ~55% ACh, 24% Glu, 14% GABA, 7% DA/OA/5-HT. Among the 613 taste-responsive neurons: 52% ACh, 25.9% GABA, 17% Glu, 2.9% 5-HT, 2.0% DA, 0.2% OA

key_findings.finding: Free, hand-set and fitted quantities: Wsyn is the single stated free parameter. It was chosen by hand so that sugar GRNs at 100 Hz give about 80% of maximal MN9 firing, i.e. tuned on the same feeding pathway that is later evaluated. All biophysical constants come from earlier papers (Kakaria & de Bivort 2017; Lazar 2021; Juergensen 2021; Paul 2015). The paper does not report several analysis choices as parameters: the stimulation frequency per experiment (10-260 Hz sweeps), the thresholds (>0 Hz counts as 'activates'; >20% drop counts as 'required'), the top-200/300 responder cut-offs, and which MN9 side is read out.
key_findings.numbers: Wsyn=0.275 mV; 100 Hz sugar -> ~80% of max MN9

key_findings.finding: The connectivity matters: when connection weights were shuffled (keeping the global weight distribution), sugar GRNs at 100 Hz almost never drove MN9, versus every time with the true connectome.
key_findings.numbers: True connectome: 100% of simulations drive MN9. Shuffled: 1 of 100 (ST1D: mean MN9_r 0.0043 Hz across 100 shuffles vs 68 Hz with correct connectivity)

key_findings.finding: Sugar-pathway predictions checked against prior experiments (Shiu, Sterne et al. eLife 2022): all 10 known sugar-responsive, PE-sufficient cell types are predicted to respond to sugar, and 8/10 are predicted to be sufficient to activate MN9. Of 5 cell types known to be required, 3 are predicted to cause a >20% MN9 drop and 1 a smaller but significant drop. Misses: Phantom (predicted inhibitory) and Usnea (possibly neuropeptidergic; Amontillado RNAi phenocopied its silencing).
key_findings.numbers: Model network: 45 neurons respond at 10 Hz and 455 at 200 Hz sugar input; 47 neurons are sugar-responsive and sufficient, 14 of them also required

key_findings.finding: New unbiased optogenetic screen (CsChrimson in SEZ split-GAL4 lines, scoring rostrum extension as the MN9 readout, n=10 flies per cell type): 106 of 138 library cell types were matched in FlyWire and activated in silico at 10-200 Hz.
key_findings.numbers: At 50 Hz: 11 predicted positive, 10 true; of 95 predicted negative, 4 positive in flies; 101/106 correct (95.3%). At 200 Hz: 5 more false positives. With glutamate set to excitatory, the false-positive rate rises from 1% to 16%

key_findings.finding: Re-analysis of ST3: base rates are low (14/106 cell types positive, where positive means any rostrum extension, even 1/10 flies). An always-'no' baseline already scores 92/106 = 86.8%. The authors' shortest-path column as a baseline: path=1 gives TP3/FP4 (85.8%); path<=2 gives TP13/FP42 (59.4%). The paper's 101/106 reproduces only when the left-MN9 column is read at 50 Hz (TP10 FP1 FN4 TN91). Right MN9 at 50 Hz gives 93.4%; left at 200 Hz 90.6%; left at 10 Hz 90.6%. Sensitivity is 10/14 and specificity 91/92.
key_findings.numbers: Always-negative 86.8%; LIF 50 Hz left 95.3%; LIF 50 Hz right 93.4%; LIF 200 Hz left 90.6%

key_findings.finding: Taste-interaction predictions tested by new optogenetics + PER: the model predicted Ir94e GRNs inhibit MN9 but, unlike bitter, cannot abolish MN9 under strong sugar. Behaviour confirmed this: Ir94e or bitter activation suppressed PER to 50 mM sucrose, and only bitter abolished PER to 1 M sucrose.
key_findings.numbers: ST9A counts with light on: Gr66a>Chrimson 3/30 PER (50 mM) and 5/30 (1 M); Ir94e>Chrimson 3/26 (50 mM) and 20/26 (1 M); n=26-32 per group

key_findings.finding: Water pathway: the model predicts large overlap between sugar and water networks (at the input level giving 40 Hz MN9). Calcium imaging confirmed water responses in Fudog and Zorro. Silencing GtACR1-expressing neurons tested 11 cell types: the main text says 5 of 6 predicted-required types were confirmed (G2N-1 failed) and 4 of 5 predicted-not-required types were confirmed (Usnea failed). Silencing sugar GRNs reduced PER to water, consistent with the predicted synergy.
key_findings.numbers: Sugar pathway 377 neurons, water 391, shared 250; sugar∩bitter 2, sugar∩Ir94e 30; 39 water-responsive sufficient neurons (30 shared with sugar); 9 necessary and sufficient

key_findings.finding: Grooming circuit (second, non-overlapping test): activating 147 JONs recovers aBN1, aBN2, aDN1 and aDN2. Only aBN1, aDN2 and 2 weak neurons drive aDN1, and only aBN1, one BN2 and aDN2 reduce aDN1 by more than 20%. New prediction: JO-CE drives aBN1 but JO-F does not, despite direct synapses. Confirmed by optogenetic activation + aBN1 calcium imaging (n>=5 flies). The prediction that silencing 3 inhibitory neurons would let JO-F drive aBN1 was explicitly left untested.
key_findings.numbers: JO-CE->aBN1 103 synapses, JO-F->aBN1 78 synapses

key_findings.finding: Headline accuracy (ST10): 150/164 predictions consistent with experiment (91.5%). Excluding the split-GAL4 screen: 49/58 (84.5%). By row: ipsi/contra 2/2; sugar-responsive 12/14; required-for-sugar 6/10; screen 101/106; bitter/Ir94e 4/4; water-responsive 8/10; required-for-water 10/11; JON-responsive 3/3; required-for-JON 2/2; JO-CE vs JO-F 2/2.

Our tally of ST10's citation columns: about 128 of the 164 predictions were scored against experiments first reported in this paper (about 122 correct), and about 36 against earlier published experiments, mostly the same lab's 2022 eLife paper (about 28 correct, ~78%). The weakest category is 'necessity' for sugar (6/10). There is also an internal inconsistency. ST10 counts G2N-1 as a correct water-silencing prediction. The main text calls it a failure, and the ST9B raw counts agree with the text: 37/50 PER under silencing vs control light-on 32/50 and 46/50. If the text is right, the totals become 149/164 (90.9%) and 48/58 (82.8%).
key_findings.numbers: New-experiment predictions ~128 (~122 correct); prior-literature ~36 (~28 correct)

key_findings.finding: Robustness (ST11): changing Wsyn by ±30% (with input rates readjusted), changing inhibitory strength relative to excitatory, or making glutamate excitatory mostly preserves the predictions. Making glutamate excitatory, however, eliminates the bitter/Ir94e inhibition result.
key_findings.numbers: Wsyn -30%: 148/164 consistent with default (90.2%), 139/164 correct (84.8%). Wsyn +30%: 156 consistent (95.1%), 144 correct (87.8%). Weaker inhibition: 156 consistent (95%), 144 correct (88%). Stronger inhibition: 158 consistent (96.3%), 146 correct (89.0%)

key_findings.finding: Runtime stated by the authors: 30 trials of 1,000 ms per experiment, Poisson-driven input neurons.
key_findings.numbers: 'approximately 5 min per 1,000 ms trial per central processing unit thread' for sugar activation, i.e. ~150 CPU-min per 30-trial condition

key_findings.finding: The paper reports no quantitative comparison against graph-traversal, signal-cascade, linear-rate or trained-network baselines. It only argues qualitatively that traversal models measure path length rather than activation and that trained DNNs need many more parameters (e.g. 734). The shuffled-weights test is the only structural null.

sources.model_or_method_spec: Inputs: FlyWire v630 proofread neuron list (127,400) and a neuron-pair table of synapse counts (Buhmann synapse detection), with a per-neuron sign from Eckstein et al. 2024 transmitter predictions (majority vote over presynaptic sites, cleft score ≥50; GABA/Glu inhibitory; ACh/DA/OA/5-HT excitatory). Stimulus: Poisson spike trains forced into chosen neurons at 10-260 Hz. Silencing: zero all outgoing weights of a neuron. Outputs: spike rates averaged over 30×1 s trials. Fixed from the literature: Vrest/Vreset -52 mV, Vth -45 mV, Tm 20 ms, tau 5 ms, refractory 2.2 ms, delay 1.8 ms. Free and hand-tuned: Wsyn = 0.275 mV, set so 100 Hz sugar input gives ~80% of max MN9. Code-only hand-set constants: f_poi = 250, so the Poisson weight is 68.75 mV and each Poisson event forces a spike; Poisson targets have no refractory period; dt is Brian2's default 0.1 ms (not set in code; my reading). Decision rules are analyst-chosen: >0 Hz MN9 = 'sufficient', MN9 ≤80% of control = 'required', 50 Hz for the screen, 40 Hz MN9-matched input for comparing pathways. No training, and no per-neuron or per-type parameters. Not modelled: gap junctions, neuromodulation, peptides, morphology, receptor kinetics, non-spiking neurons, internal state, basal activity.
sources.validation_design: Single connectome (one female FlyWire brain, v630). There is no held-out individual, stage or second connectome. Validation is qualitative and binary (responds or not, sufficient or not, required or not), scored against: (a) earlier experiments, mostly the same lab's Shiu, Sterne et al. eLife 2022, which were known when the model was built (~36 predictions); and (b) new experiments in this paper (~128 predictions): an unbiased optogenetic split-GAL4 screen of 106 SEZ cell types (rostrum extension, n=10 flies each), PER under bitter/Ir94e optogenetic activation (n=26-32), GtACR1 water-silencing of 11 cell types (n=30-50), calcium imaging of Fudog and Zorro, and JO-CE/JO-F→aBN1 functional connectivity imaging (n≥5). Wsyn was tuned on sugar→MN9, which belongs to the evaluated feeding circuit; the screen and grooming circuit were not used for tuning. The metric is fraction of consistent predictions. No AUROC/AUPRC, no class-balanced metric, and no comparison with simple graph baselines. Absolute firing rates are explicitly not claimed to be accurate. Nulls and robustness: 100 weight shuffles; Wsyn ±30%; inhibition strength relative to excitation ±50%; glutamate made excitatory.
stated_limitations: Zero basal firing means inhibition onto silent neurons has no effect, so disinhibition circuits are poorly modelled (Phantom and Tentacular failures)
No neuromodulation, neuropeptides or extrasynaptic signalling (Usnea failure; neuropeptide involvement suggested by Amontillado RNAi)
No gap junctions (not identifiable in EM), no non-spiking neurons, no internal state
Every neuron is an identical point neuron; morphology and receptor dynamics are ignored
Assumes each neuron is entirely excitatory or entirely inhibitory; glutamate assumed inhibitory, and the result depends on this
Accuracy is limited by the accuracy of synapse detection and transmitter prediction
Absolute firing rates are unlikely to be accurate; only broad differences across a range of input rates are interpreted
Precise dynamics may be poorly simulated
Connectivity constrains but does not dictate circuit mechanism (citing C. elegans and STG work)
Only the feeding circuit is complete in the volume; circuits that need descending neurons or the VNC are incomplete in FlyWire
Left-hemisphere GRN reconstructions are more complete, so simulations were mostly unilateral; the FAFB left/right inversion is noted
sources.code: https://github.com/philshiu/Drosophila_brain_model. MIT licence, confirmed via the GitHub API (spdx MIT; LICENSE reads 'Copyright (c) 2023 Philip Shiu and Nico Spiller'). Python 3.10, Brian2 2.5.1, pandas, pyarrow, joblib. Fully CPU; see the separate repository entry for details.

sources.novelty_threat_for_m08: Strong pre-emption of three claims: (1) a structure-only, untrained spiking model built from connectome synapse counts plus transmitter signs, with one global free parameter, predicts which neurons respond to, are sufficient for, and are required for a sensorimotor output, with independent wet-lab confirmation (~91% of 164); (2) in-silico activation and single-neuron silencing screens to discover circuits; (3) shuffled-connectivity nulls and Wsyn/I:E/glutamate robustness. M08 must call any rerun of this a replication. Not pre-empted: compact generative or compressed wiring rules (Shiu uses the exact wiring list), transfer across individuals or connectomes, baseline-parity tests against graph or linear models, class-balanced metrics, and building circuits from capability constraints (G-CONSTRUCT).
sources.gaps_m08_could_test: (1) Baseline parity on the frozen 106-cell-type screen (ST3 has observed rates, LIF rates per frequency and side, and shortest path): signed linear propagation, weighted k-hop signed path sums, probabilistic graph traversal, an always-negative baseline. Report balanced accuracy and AUPRC with the 14/106 base rate, and pre-register the frequency/side/threshold choices whose variation moves accuracy between 90.6% and 95.3%. (2) Structured nulls between 'true wiring' and 'global shuffle': degree-preserving, sign-preserving, within-cell-type and within-hop rewiring, and cell-type stochastic block models fitted to the SEZ sub-circuit. The question is how much predictive power a compact generative rule keeps (H0-TOPO / H1-GENERATE). (3) Sub-circuit sufficiency: is MN9 behaviour preserved when only the SEZ feeding subnetwork is simulated? (4) Transfer: run the frozen model and Wsyn on v783 or another connectome (BANC, male CNS) and re-score the 164 predictions, covering cross-individual and cross-version robustness. (5) Sign-noise sensitivity using the per-neuron transmitter-confidence distribution. Wet-lab-only predictions (e.g. silencing 3 inhibitory neurons lets JO-F drive aBN1) cannot be tested by M08.

Inspected sez_neurons.pickle with pickletools (disassembly only, never unpickled). Read the issue list and commit history, plus the issue #6, #7, #10, #11 threads.

key_findings.finding: Bundled data: v630 (used in the paper) and v783 (public, added Sept 2024). Each is a neuron list plus a neuron-pair table with columns Presynaptic_ID, Postsynaptic_ID, Presynaptic_Index, Postsynaptic_Index, Connectivity, Excitatory, 'Excitatory x Connectivity'. Synapse counts per pair start at 1 (no minimum-synapse threshold).
key_findings.numbers: v630: 127,400 neurons, 14,687,178 connected pairs, synapses/pair 1-2,358, signed weights -2,358..+1,801. v783: 138,639 neurons, 15,091,983 pairs, synapses/pair 1-2,405. Files: v630 parquet 86,630,944 B; v630 csv 3,057,611 B; v783 parquet 100,804,642 B; v783 csv 3,327,347 B; repo size field 189,741 KB

key_findings.finding: Implementation: Brian2 NeuronGroup (method='linear'; 'unless refractory' on both v and g) plus one Synapses object with a homogeneous 1.8 ms delay and w = signed count × w_syn. PoissonInput adds w_syn×f_poi = 68.75 mV directly to v, so each event is effectively a forced spike. Silencing zeroes outgoing weights only (README says 'to and from'; the paper says 'all output', so code and paper agree). Each trial rebuilds the full network from CSV+parquet. The 30 trials run in parallel with joblib/loky; figures.ipynb used n_proc=15.
key_findings.numbers: t_run 1000 ms, n_run 30, default r_poi 150 Hz, f_poi 250

key_findings.finding: Reproducibility coverage: figures.ipynb has code for Fig. 1D-F, 2, 3, 4a-c,e, 5b-d,g and Figs. S1D and S4. Keyword search found no code for the 100-shuffle control (ST1D), the Wsyn/inhibition/glutamate robustness analyses (ST11), or the GRN clustering. There is no pipeline that builds the connectivity tables from FlyWire (issue #6; the author then supplied v783 files). Neuron IDs change between versions: v630 IDs fail on v783 (issue #7).

My count of experiment conditions in figures.ipynb: ~11,000 conditions × 30 trials ≈ 330,000 one-second trials to regenerate every main figure. At the paper's ~5 CPU-min/trial that is ≈27,500 CPU-hours. Most of the cost is per-neuron activation (8 freqs × 200-300 neurons) and silencing sweeps.
key_findings.numbers: Fig1E 1,600; Fig1F 1,600; Fig2 424; Fig3 242; Fig4b 1,600; Fig4c 1,400; Fig4e 154; Fig5c 2,400; Fig5d 1,500; other ~100 conditions

read:shiu.summary_for_m08:
I read the full text of Shiu et al. Nature 2024 via the Europe PMC XML (PMC11446845, CC BY 4.0), plus the Supplementary Tables xlsx (2.5 MB) and the code repo. The paper is a strong precedent for the Drosophila functional line, but it is not a generative-law result.

What it is. An untrained whole-brain leaky integrate-and-fire model over FlyWire v630: 127,400 neurons and 14,687,178 connected neuron pairs (my count from the repo's neuron list and parquet footer). Each weight is synapse count × per-neuron sign × Wsyn. The sign comes from the majority vote of Eckstein transmitter predictions, with GABA and glutamate treated as inhibitory. Biophysical constants come from earlier papers (Vth−Vrest = 7 mV, tau_m = 20 ms, tau_syn = 5 ms, refractory 2.2 ms, delay 1.8 ms). The one stated free parameter is Wsyn = 0.275 mV, hand-tuned on sugar→MN9, which is part of the evaluated feeding circuit. There are also unreported analysis choices: input frequency, the >0 Hz and 20%-drop thresholds, the top-200/300 cut-offs, which MN9 side is read out, and the code constant f_poi = 250 (each Poisson event forces a spike).

What was validated. 164 binary predictions, 150 consistent (91.5%); 49/58 (84.5%) without the split-GAL4 screen. By my tally of ST10, about 128 predictions were scored against new experiments (~122 correct) and about 36 against the same lab's earlier data (~28 correct). The new experiments were:
- an unbiased CsChrimson screen of 106 SEZ cell types (rostrum extension, n = 10 flies each), 101/106 correct;
- PER behaviour showing bitter and Ir94e are both aversive but only bitter can abolish PER to 1 M sucrose;
- GtACR1 water-silencing of 11 cell types;
- calcium imaging of Fudog and Zorro;
- JO-CE vs JO-F → aBN1 functional-connectivity imaging.

The weakest category is necessity for sugar (6/10). ST10 also counts G2N-1 as correct while the main text and the raw counts say it failed; if the text is right, the totals are 149/164 and 48/58.

Baseline gaps (my recomputation from ST3).
- The screen has a 14/106 positive base rate, so always predicting 'no extension' already scores 86.8%.
- The paper's 101/106 (sensitivity 10/14, specificity 91/92) reproduces only with left MN9 at 50 Hz. Right MN9 gives 93.4%; 200 Hz gives 90.6%.
- Shortest-path baselines score 85.8% (path = 1) and 59.4% (path ≤ 2).
- The only structural null is a global weight shuffle (1/100 shuffles drive MN9 vs 100% with the true connectome). No intermediate nulls (degree-, type- or sign-preserving) and no linear-model or graph-traversal comparisons were reported.
- One connectome only: no held-out individual or stage.
- Robustness was tested: ±30% Wsyn gives 85-88% accuracy, ±50% inhibition gives 88-89%. Making glutamate excitatory abolishes the bitter/Ir94e result and raises screen false positives from 1% to 16%.
- Stated limitations: zero basal firing (so disinhibition fails, e.g. Phantom and Tentacular), and no neuromodulation, peptides, gap junctions or morphology. A 2026 Nature Communications paper (Savaş et al.) shows a feeding-circuit neuron pair acting through both a peptide and acetylcholine, against the one-neuron-one-sign assumption.

Code and data. GitHub philshiu/Drosophila_brain_model: MIT (GitHub API), Python 3.10 + Brian2 2.5.1, CPU only. It bundles the v630 and v783 tables (86.6 / 100.8 MB parquet, above the Gate-1 limit, not downloaded). figures.ipynb regenerates the main figures. There is no code for the shuffle or robustness analyses and no pipeline that builds the tables from FlyWire. The README says silencing cuts inputs and outputs; the code cuts outputs only, which matches the paper. Model outputs are on Edmond (doi:10.17617/3.CZODIW, MIT, results.zip 4.5 GB). Third-party v783 reports (unreviewed GitHub issues) describe a GABAergic neuron (il3LN6) signed excitatory, which triggers an ~8,300-neuron runaway state. So reproduce on v630 and treat signs as uncertain.

Compute.
- The paper reports ~5 CPU-min per 1 s trial and uses 30 trials per condition.
- An Eon Systems Brian2 C++ standalone port reports ~2.9 s simulated time per 1 s trial (CPU model not stated).
- Regenerating every main figure is ~11,000 conditions × 30 trials ≈ 330k trials. That is ≈27,500 CPU-h at the paper's rate, or ~200+ h at the C++ standalone rate (my estimates).
- Memory is likely 2-4 GB per worker (estimate).

A sensible small CPU test for M08 has four steps.
1. Freeze v630, all parameters and Wsyn. Pre-register the readout rules (50 Hz, a fixed MN9 side, >0 Hz).
2. Reproduce the 106-cell-type screen (3,180 trials; ~265 CPU-h at the paper's rate, or ~2-3 h with C++ standalone).
3. Crop to the SEZ→MN9 sub-circuit (neurons on short paths) and check that the predictions survive.
4. Compare, with balanced accuracy and AUPRC: an always-negative baseline, shortest-path and signed-weighted-path baselines, a signed linear-rate model, degree-, type- and sign-preserving rewirings, and a compact cell-type block-model generator replacing the true wiring.

The question is how much of the functional prediction a compressible rule keeps (H1/H2 vs H0-TOPO/H0-KNOWN). Cross-version or cross-connectome re-scoring of the 164 predictions (v783 / BANC / male CNS) would be the transfer test.

Novelty threat. The paper (and Sapkal 2024, Pugliese 2025, Özdil 2026) already covers connectome-plus-sign LIF models predicting sufficient and required neurons with wet-lab confirmation, in-silico activation and silencing screens, minimal-circuit pruning and shuffle nulls; anything there would be a replication. Not covered: compact generative wiring rules, cross-individual transfer, baseline parity and G-CONSTRUCT. G-FUNCTION evidence is feasible without new experiments by re-scoring the published binary outcomes (ST3 and ST9-ST10). Untested wet-lab predictions, such as silencing the three inhibitory neurons that block JO-F from driving aBN1, are out of reach.

sources.citation: Dorkenwald S, Matsliah A, Sterling AR, Schlegel P, Yu S-c, et al. (FlyWire Consortium). Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain. Nature 634, 124-138 (2024). doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07558-y. PMC11446842. Licence of article: CC BY 4.0.
sources.url: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07558-y (nature.com redirected to an idp login; full text read from Europe PMC XML: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC11446842/fullTextXML)
sources.what_was_read: Read all of the main text, Discussion (including the 'Limitations of our reconstruction' section), all Methods, and the Data and Code availability statements, from the Europe PMC full-text XML. Extended Data and Supplementary figures were read only as captions. Supplementary Fig. 2 (per-neuropil attachment) and the Supplementary tables were not read.

key_findings.finding: Release 783 is the second public release. The paper's analyses use v783: 139,255 proofread neurons, a central brain plus both optic lobes, one adult female (FAFB volume, ssTEM at 4x4x40 nm). Annotations in Codex and elsewhere carry the true biological side, but the FAFB images were acquired left-right inverted, so images and meshes stay mirrored.
key_findings.numbers: 139,255 neurons; 54.5M synapses between neurons; v783 took 3,013,513 edits and about 33 person-years of proofreading

key_findings.finding: Synapses come from automatic detection (Buhmann et al. 2021, scored with the Heinrich et al. cleft segmentation) and were never manually proofread. Filtering kept synapses with cleft score >50, both ends assigned to a segment, and duplicates within 100 nm removed. The detector was trained only on the CREMI ground truth (3 cubes of 5x5x5 µm from the calyx, 1,965 synapses). Performance varies by region and is worse for some cell types, especially sensory neurons.
key_findings.numbers: about 244M raw synapses reduced to about 130M after filtering

key_findings.finding: Completeness is asymmetric. Presynapses attach to proofread neurons at a high rate and postsynapses at a much lower rate. False negatives are the main error type, but false positives exist too, so the authors recommend thresholding. Codex and the paper use a threshold of 5 synapses per pair. Matsliah et al. found 2 synapses appropriate in the optic lobe. Raising postsynaptic attachment from 44.7% to 50% would need >700,000 more fragments proofread. Nearly all connections with more than 9 synapses are detected.
key_findings.numbers: presynapse attachment 93.7% (about 122M); postsynapse attachment 44.7% (about 58.1M); 2,700,513 connections with ≥5 synapses among 134,181 neurons

key_findings.finding: Proofreading accuracy was checked by re-proofreading a random sample of 826 central-brain neurons.
key_findings.numbers: mean F1 = 99.2% by volume

key_findings.finding: Neurotransmitter predictions come from Eckstein et al. and cover 6 classes: ACh, Glu, GABA, 5-HT, DA, OA. The authors assume Dale's law, assign each neuron a single transmitter, and treat ACh as excitatory and GABA/Glu as inhibitory. They state that a prediction 'could be wrong' for any individual synapse.
key_findings.numbers: per-synapse accuracy 87%; per-neuron accuracy 94% (quoted from Eckstein et al.)

key_findings.finding: Other stated limitations: no electrical synapses; the left lamina is partially severed from the medulla, which lowers accuracy for some left lamina neurons; afferent axons are truncated; the brain was not connected to the VNC.

Data availability: Codex, braincircuits.io and CATMAID Spaces for interactive use; 'most of the data' downloadable from codex.flywire.ai/api/download; programmatic access through CAVE and cloudvolume; Zenodo dumps of connectivity (10.5281/zenodo.10676866) and information-flow results (10.5281/zenodo.12588557). Code: CAVEconnectome and murthylab/codex.

sources.validation_design: This is a resource paper. Validation consists of re-proofreading 826 random neurons (volumetric F1), comparing attachment rates with the hemibrain and between hemispheres, and checking left-right symmetry of the projectome. The cross-brain cell-type and edge comparison is deferred to Schlegel et al. No held-out functional validation. The information-flow model is descriptive.
stated_limitations: Synapses were not manually proofread; detection was trained only on calyx ground truth; sensory neurons are particularly affected
Postsynaptic attachment is only 44.7%, so weak connections are undercounted and some are missed
The threshold of 5 synapses is 'reasonable but arbitrary'; the synapse-count distribution has no bimodality to justify a threshold
Only chemical synapses; gap junctions are not captured
The left lamina is partially severed (a one-sided artefact)
Neurotransmitter assignment assumes Dale's law, but co-transmission is known to occur
The connectome is a single female brain; sex differences and mushroom-body variability are noted
sources.code: CAVE (github.com/CAVEconnectome) and Codex (github.com/murthylab/codex). We checked the Codex licence via the GitHub API: Apache-2.0. Python, CPU-only. Codex's open-source loader (codex/data/local_data_loader.py) fetches anonymously from https://storage.googleapis.com/flywire-data/codex/data/fafb/{version}/{file}.
sources.data: Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.10676866 (checked via the Zenodo API: version 783.0, published 2024-06-02, licence cc-by-4.0, access_right open, no login needed). Files: flywire_synapses_783.feather 9,492,998,242 B; proofread_connections_783.feather 852,022,274 B; per_neuron_neuropil_count_post_783.feather 233,843,050 B; per_neuron_neuropil_count_pre_783.feather 16,853,770 B; proofread_root_ids_783.npy 1,114,168 B. Only one version exists in the record's version list (no 630 version). Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.12588557: information-flow ranks, cc-by-4.0, 17 feather files of about 1.4-1.6 MB each.
sources.novelty_threat_for_m08: No generative or developmental model, so there is no direct threat to a G-STRUCT generator claim. However, the information-flow traversal model (Schlegel 2021 algorithm, run 10,000 times per seed set) is a known compact 'structure → functional ordering' descriptor and must be treated as an existing baseline. The paper also states that one wild-type brain 'should be useful for studying any' individual. That stereotypy claim is the authors' and limits how novel any cross-individual 'regularity' finding can be.
sources.gaps_m08_could_test: (1) Robustness of any structural rule to the synapse threshold (1/2/5/10) and to the asymmetric pre/post attachment. Simulate missing postsynapses at the per-neuropil attachment rates in Codex's synapse_attachment_rates.csv.gz before claiming a rule. (2) Left-versus-right hemisphere of the same brain as a first, cheap held-out 'individual'. Its known correlation (Schlegel) limits it to a weak test. (3) Excluding the left lamina from any optic-lobe held-out test because of the severing artefact.

sources.citation: Schlegel P, Yin Y, Bates AS, Dorkenwald S, Eichler K, et al., Jefferis GSXE. Whole-brain annotation and multi-connectome cell typing of Drosophila. Nature 634, 139-152 (2024). doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07686-5. PMC11446831. Licence of article: CC BY 4.0.
sources.what_was_read: Read the abstract, all Results sections, and the full Discussion (including 'Which edges are important?' and 'Have we collected a snowflake?'). In Methods, read: base annotations, soma side, biological outliers and sample artefacts, high-resolution skeletonization, connectivity normalization, connectivity stereotypy analyses, CATMAID Spaces, synapse counts, the technical noise model, and Data and Code availability. Not read in detail: the hemilineage annotation methods, the NBLAST and co-clustering algorithm details, the KC rate-model methods, and the statistics section.

key_findings.finding: The paper provides a hierarchical annotation (flow > superclass > class > cell type, plus hemilineage) for all 139,255 v783 neurons, and a consensus cell-type atlas.
key_findings.numbers: 8,453 cell types, covering 96.4% of neurons; 3,643 consensus types matched to the hemibrain; 4,581 new types; 98% of central-brain neurons given a terminal type; 32% (1,651) of hemibrain types could not be reidentified

key_findings.finding: Developmental annotation: 120 neuroblast lineages and 183 hemilineages cover 88% (30,233) of central-brain neurons, with neuron counts per hemilineage very precise between sides and across brains.
key_findings.numbers: left-right count difference 3% (±4%); FlyWire versus hemibrain hemilineage counts R² = 0.98; FlyWire has about 5% more neurons

key_findings.finding: Edge reliability across three hemispheres (FlyWire left, FlyWire right, hemibrain). Edges are generally reproducible, and strong edges almost always so.
key_findings.numbers: 53% of hemibrain edges are found in FlyWire; FlyWire left→right 61%, right→left 59%; a 1-synapse hemibrain edge is found in one FlyWire hemisphere 42% of the time and in both 16%; edges >10 synapses are >90% reproducible (16% of edges but about 79% of synapses); normalized weight ≥0.9% of target input is >90% persistent (about 7% of edges, 54% of synapses); 'strong' = >2.6% or 31 synapses gives 99% persistence; edge-weight correlation R = 0.97 within a brain and 0.80 across brains

key_findings.finding: Technical-noise model: fictive ground truth scaled by per-neuropil postsynaptic completion, then resampled using synapse-detection precision 0.72 and recall 0.77. On average it explains 65% of the observed left-right edge-weight variability (close to 100% for weak edges). The authors conclude that edge-weight differences of ≤30% may be purely technical.
key_findings.numbers: 500 rounds; analysis limited to edges of 1-30 synapses

key_findings.finding: Variability in the mushroom body. FlyWire has about 30% more Kenyon cells per hemisphere than the hemibrain. KCg-m cells compensate by sampling fewer ALPN types (K) while keeping the E/I ratio. A rate model shows the optimal K is lower in FlyWire. The authors describe this as homeostatic compensation through a single parameter.
key_findings.numbers: Kenyon cells: 2,597 (FlyWire right), 2,580 (FlyWire left), 1,917 (hemibrain); K for KCg-m: 5.74, 5.89, 8.76

key_findings.finding: The Discussion argues that cell typing compresses the graph (131,811 typed nodes to 8,453 type nodes). Linking to the 'genomic bottleneck' idea, it says lossy compression (type nodes, strong edges approximated, weak edges largely ignored) would cut storage 'by orders of magnitude'. This is not tested as a generator.

About 0.4% of central-brain neurons show biological oddities, recorded as outlier_bio. Neurons with dark-cytosol or segmentation artefacts (outlier_seg) were excluded from connectivity analyses. These artefacts are more frequent in sensory neurons.

Access statement: 'At the time of writing, access to Codex and CAVE requires signing up using a Google account.' Annotations are on GitHub (flyconnectome/flywire_annotations). NBLAST scores and skeletons are on Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.10877326; connectivity is on Zenodo 10676866.

sources.validation_design: Hemibrain cell types are treated as predictions and tested by reidentification in two FlyWire hemispheres from a different animal and EM modality. Cell types are cross-validated across three hemispheres. New two-hemisphere types are tested by adding the hemibrain as a third: 70% survive with minor edits, 84% if single-neuron moves are ignored. Edge persistence is measured across hemispheres, and the technical-noise model gives a lower bound on biological variability.
stated_limitations: Only two brains (three hemispheres); the two FlyWire hemispheres are not independent, and variability can be correlated across them
Hemibrain truncation confounds matching
Daisy-chain ambiguities between similar types
Synapse-count comparisons are confounded by different completion and detection rates between datasets
Edges below the reliability thresholds may still matter functionally
Kenyon cells, VPNs, ORNs and outlier_seg types were excluded from the stereotypy analyses
sources.code: navis (navis-org/navis), fafbseg-py (navis-org/fafbseg-py; licence checked via the GitHub API: GPL-3.0), cocoa, natverse coconatfly. CPU-feasible.
sources.data: github.com/flyconnectome/flywire_annotations. The GitHub API reports licence = None (no LICENSE file). The Zenodo mirror of release v3.2.0 (10.5281/zenodo.23037340, 2026-09-29) is tagged cc-by-4.0, zip 12,153,637 B. Main file: supplemental_files/Supplemental_file1_neuron_annotations.tsv, 31,720,298 B, with root_id (783), flow, super_class, cell_class, cell_sub_class, cell_type, hemibrain_type, ito_lee_hemilineage, hartenstein_hemilineage, top_nt, top_nt_conf, side, status, fru_dsx, synonyms, dimorphism, supertype. Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.10877326 (cc-by-4.0): NBLAST feathers of 212-809 MB and a skeletons parquet of 5,355,543,468 B. Release history: v1.x was based on segmentation 630; v2.0.0 and later on 783; v2.1.0 matches the 2024 papers; v3.0-3.1 adds MaleCNS cross-validation and retypes JO neurons; v3.2.0 retypes the GRNs.
sources.novelty_threat_for_m08: High for any M08 claim that 'a compact type-level description generates/compresses the fly connectome' or that 'strong edges are the reproducible core'. The compression and genomic-bottleneck argument, the edge-reliability heuristics (>10 synapses, ≥0.9%, 2.6%/31 synapses) and the technical-noise model already exist. The KC 'single-parameter (K) compensation' is a published developmental-compensation rule. Hemilineage and morphology-group regularities are documented. M08 may only call these 'reproduced' unless it goes beyond them.
sources.gaps_m08_could_test: (1) Use Schlegel's cross-hemisphere and cross-brain edge persistence as the empirical ceiling for any edge-prediction score: a generator cannot be expected to beat inter-individual reproducibility, and reporting AUPRC relative to that ceiling is a fair, strong reference. (2) Actually build and score the compressed type-level generator the authors only describe (types + strong-edge probabilities), with an MDL (minimum description length) proxy, then test on held-out hemispheres or brains (hemibrain, BANC, MCNS). This is a real test they did not run. (3) Test whether hemilineage identity (a developmental proxy) predicts connectivity beyond cell type and space. Hemilineage labels for 88% of central-brain neurons make this feasible. (4) Bake the ≤30% technical-noise band into the null model.

sources.citation: FlyWire Codex documentation: FAQ (https://codex.flywire.ai/faq), About FlyWire (https://codex.flywire.ai/about_flywire), landing and download portal (https://codex.flywire.ai/api/download, ?dataset=fafb). Accessed 2026-10-25.
sources.what_was_read: Fetched the raw HTML of the FAQ, the About FlyWire page and the landing page, and read their full text. The download portal (/api/download and /api/download?dataset=fafb) returns only the 'Sign in to browse brain maps' landing page, so the actual list of files, sizes and citation text behind sign-in was NOT accessible. No sign-in or token was used.

key_findings.finding: Snapshots: FAFB default 783 ('v783 - Oct 2023 [latest release]'). Version 630 is no longer offered in the Codex selector. Other datasets: BANC v888 (May 20 2026) and v626 (Jul 20 2025); MANC v1.2.1; MAOL v1.1; MCNS v1.0 and v0.9. The landing page shows FAFB v783 with 139,255 neurons and 3,732,460 connections.
key_findings.numbers: FAFB 139,255 neurons / 3,732,460 connections; BANC v888 158,262 neurons; MCNS v1.0 166,700 neurons; MAOL v1.1 52,445 neurons

key_findings.finding: Bulk downloads (static CSVs) are offered only for the FlyWire datasets (FAFB, BANC). Every download request needs an api_token copied from the user's Codex account page (Google sign-in). Codex 'intentionally does not provide a general programmatic live-query API'. Named data products include consolidated_cell_types and connections_princeton. Portal files are synced to current Codex data and 'may differ from original publication-time archives'.
Default connection thresholds: FAFB 5+, BANC 3+, MANC 1+, MAOL 1+, MCNS 5+. The Connectivity and Pathways tools cannot go below these. Connection tables have one row per pair per neuropil.

The About page says synapses are now 'automatically detected using Yu et al.', and that synapses originally released before July 2025 were predicted with Buhmann et al. and refined with Heinrich et al. Hierarchical annotations come from Schlegel et al.; neurotransmitter predictions from Eckstein, Bates et al. Annotations are updated in Codex 'about weekly'.

Predicted and verified neurotransmitter fields may disagree. The FAQ says to treat predicted fields as model output and verified fields as curated. A CAVE token is needed for root-ID mapping across versions. Root IDs change when a neuron is edited.

Circuit tools available after sign-in: structured search with {upstream}/{downstream}, {upstream_region}/{downstream_region}, {pathways} =>, connectivity graphs with CSV/JSON export 'when small enough', Pathways (shortest paths with an avoid query), and 3-node Motifs.
